item.content:encoded: Escambia County Sheriff's Office responded to West Florida High School on Thursday after receiving reports of a bomb threat and active-shooter threat, according to WKRG News 5. The school was placed on lockdown as deputies investigated the reports. The lockdown has since been lifted, and officials have provided no additional details about the nature of the threats or whether any devices were found. The sheriff's office has not released information about whether arrests have been made or if the investigation remains ongoing.

item.title: Pensacola Hurricane Isaias Public Damage and Recovery Costs Top $47 Million
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: PENSACOLA, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- The City of Pensacola now estimates Hurricane Isaias caused more than $47 million in damage to public facilities and government recovery costs, while crews continue a debris operation expected to last several more weeks. The latest assessment includes approximately $16 million in projected debris-removal costs.…
item.content:encoded:
PENSACOLA, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- The City of Pensacola now estimates Hurricane Isaias caused more than $47 million in damage to public facilities and government recovery costs, while crews continue a debris operation expected to last several more weeks.

The latest assessment includes approximately $16 million in projected debris-removal costs.

Another $24.5 million involves damage to city-owned buildings, parks and other facilities, including Pensacola International Airport, the Port of Pensacola, fire stations and community facilities.

The figure is separate from the city's earlier estimate of more than $71 million in damage to privately owned property.

The new federal Major Disaster Declaration means eligible city expenses can now qualify for FEMA Public Assistance.

Reeves said the federal reimbursement could cover roughly $12 million of the city's projected $16 million debris bill.

Pensacola has collected approximately 347,000 cubic yards of hurricane debris so far.

About two-thirds of city roads have received at least some debris collection, although city officials emphasize that does not mean those streets are finished.

The contractor estimates it will take approximately three more weeks to complete the first full collection pass.

A second pass will begin immediately afterward.

The city has also established a dedicated debris hotline at 833-495-3573 for residents with questions about pickup, eligible debris and how material should be prepared.

The hotline operates from 7 a.m. until 7 p.m., seven days a week.

FEMA Individual Assistance for residents remains under federal review.

item.title: Daylight Saving Time Ends Sunday: AAA Warns of Evening Commute Hazards
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: When clocks fall back an hour early Sunday morning, November 1, drivers across the Panhandle will face shifting visibility challenges that could increase crash risk, according to AAA — The Auto Club Group. The end of daylight saving time means sunset will arrive roughly an hour earlier, pushing more evening commutes into darkness. Research from…
item.content:encoded:
When clocks fall back an hour early Sunday morning, November 1, drivers across the Panhandle will face shifting visibility challenges that could increase crash risk, according to AAA — The Auto Club Group.

The end of daylight saving time means sunset will arrive roughly an hour earlier, pushing more evening commutes into darkness. Research from the AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety shows pedestrian fatalities have climbed dramatically since 2009, with nearly all that increase occurring after dark, particularly on busy city roads. The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety also found pedestrian deaths spike when standard time resumes, highlighting the heightened danger for walkers and cyclists in low-light conditions.

"Drivers can expect a noticeable change in their commute almost overnight," said Mark Jenkins, AAA spokesman for The Auto Club Group. "Morning sun glare can make it difficult to see the road ahead, while earlier darkness makes pedestrians and cyclists harder to spot in the evening. Slow down, leave extra space and stay focused, especially around intersections and crosswalks."

AAA recommends checking headlights, taillights, and turn signals before evening drives, keeping sunglasses accessible for morning glare, and reducing speed after dark to stay within the beam of your headlights. The time change also coincides with increased drowsy-driving risk—the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration linked 644 deaths to fatigue-related crashes in 2024. If you feel drowsy behind the wheel, pull over safely to rest rather than push through fatigue.

item.title: Former Pensacola Officer Faces Additional Charges in Ongoing Investigation
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: A former Pensacola Police Department officer already facing serious charges related to drug possession and child exploitation material has been accused of an additional crime: taking photos of adult men in bathroom stalls without consent, according to arrest documents reviewed by local media. The allegations compound an already troubling case…
item.content:encoded:
A former Pensacola Police Department officer already facing serious charges related to drug possession and child exploitation material has been accused of an additional crime: taking photos of adult men in bathroom stalls without consent, according to arrest documents reviewed by local media.

The allegations compound an already troubling case involving the officer, who was arrested on charges of possessing child sexual abuse material, bestiality videos, and drug paraphernalia. The bathroom surveillance allegations suggest a pattern of behavior investigators are working to fully document.

The Pensacola Police Department and state authorities have not yet released detailed public statements about the scope of the investigation or whether additional charges are expected. The case remains under active review, and investigators may be pursuing further leads.

The gathering, scheduled from 6:00 p.m. to 7:30 p.m., comes ahead of the 2027 Florida Legislative Session and gives constituents a chance to weigh in on local priorities. The meeting will be held at…
item.content:encoded:
The Escambia County Legislative Delegation will host its annual public meeting on Thursday, November 12, 2026, at The Beach Church on Pensacola Beach. The gathering, scheduled from 6:00 p.m. to 7:30 p.m., comes ahead of the 2027 Florida Legislative Session and gives constituents a chance to weigh in on local priorities.

The meeting will be held at The Beach Church, 920 Panferio Drive on Pensacola Beach. According to North Escambia reporting, the annual forum allows community members to present issues and concerns to the delegation before lawmakers head to Tallahassee for the next legislative session.

The delegation typically uses these public meetings to gather feedback on education, infrastructure, public safety, and other matters affecting Escambia County before introducing bills and priorities at the state level.

item.content:encoded:
The Tate High School FFA Chapter has captured first place in the Florida Turfgrass Science Invitational Student Competition, held at Candler Hills Golf Course at On Top of the World in Ocala. The win advances the team to nationals competition.

The championship team included Baylor Touchstone, Addyson Smallwood, Allison Wynne, and Cade McNair. The competition tests students' knowledge and skills in turfgrass management and science across a range of practical and theoretical challenges.

This marks another state title for the Tate High FFA program, which continues to establish itself as a competitive force in agricultural education across Escambia County.

The Extra Mile Club Str8 Up will receive $349,650 annually—totaling $1,048,950 over three years—to…
item.content:encoded:
The Escambia County Children's Trust board this week approved $3.6 million in yearly funding for community youth and family programs across the county, including more than $1 million over three years for a new learning and readiness hub in Century.

The Extra Mile Club Str8 Up will receive $349,650 annually—totaling $1,048,950 over three years—to operate the "Soul Train Little Learners & Family Readiness Hub" in Century. The hub is designed to serve early learners and families in the North Escambia area.

The broader funding package, approved this week, directs more than $3.6 million per year to various youth-focused initiatives across Escambia County. The Children's Trust, a county agency, oversees investments in early childhood development, after-school programs, family support services, and related community initiatives.

item.title: Defense seeks to toss evidence in Nesmith vehicular homicide case
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Attorneys for Greg Nesmith, a former Escambia County Sheriff's deputy facing vehicular homicide charges in the deaths of two 20-year-olds on Perdido Key, are asking a judge to invalidate his arrest warrant and suppress evidence they say was gathered through a misleading investigation, according to court filings. The legal challenge represents a…
item.content:encoded:
Attorneys for Greg Nesmith, a former Escambia County Sheriff's deputy facing vehicular homicide charges in the deaths of two 20-year-olds on Perdido Key, are asking a judge to invalidate his arrest warrant and suppress evidence they say was gathered through a misleading investigation, according to court filings.

The legal challenge represents a significant procedural hurdle in the case against Nesmith. Defense lawyers have argued that the investigative process that led to his arrest contained improper conduct, potentially undermining the reliability of evidence prosecutors plan to use at trial.

Nesmith is accused in connection with a fatal crash on Perdido Key that claimed the lives of two young adults. The case has drawn attention given Nesmith's background in law enforcement. A hearing on the defense motion has not yet been scheduled in Escambia County courts.

item.title: Visit Pensacola Reports $1.3B Tourism Impact, Installs New CEO Tony Lyle
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Visit Pensacola celebrated a strong fiscal year at its annual meeting Wednesday, reporting $1.3 billion in direct visitor spending and welcoming new leadership as the organization charts its next phase of growth for Escambia County's tourism economy. Tony Lyle has assumed the role of President and CEO, replacing outgoing leadership as the…
item.content:encoded:
Visit Pensacola celebrated a strong fiscal year at its annual meeting Wednesday, reporting $1.3 billion in direct visitor spending and welcoming new leadership as the organization charts its next phase of growth for Escambia County's tourism economy.

Tony Lyle has assumed the role of President and CEO, replacing outgoing leadership as the destination marketing organization focuses on elevating Pensacola's profile nationally and internationally. Lyle told community leaders and tourism partners gathered at the meeting that he sees significant opportunity to build on the region's momentum. "There's tremendous momentum here, driven by an incredible team, strong industry partnerships, and a community that takes pride in what makes this destination unique," Lyle said.

FY2026 numbers underscore the sector's reach and economic muscle. Visit Pensacola welcomed nearly 2.6 million visitors, generated more than $23.6 million in Tourism Development Tax collections, and booked more than 2.6 million room nights. The organization's digital footprint expanded substantially, reaching 3.6 million visitors on VisitPensacola.com and growing social media followers to over 554,000 across nine platforms.

Outgoing Board Chair Capt. Sterling Gilliam, USN (ret.), director of the National Naval Aviation Museum, praised the team's execution during the leadership transition. "The accomplishments we're celebrating today are a direct reflection of their hard work and the strength of our tourism community," Gilliam said, noting confidence in the organization's future under Lyle's direction.

item.title: Living Museum brings 467 years of Pensacola history to life at Foo Foo Festival
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Pensacola's past will take center stage next week when Fiesta Pensacola presents its Living Museum experience as part of the Foo Foo Festival. The immersive event Thursday, Nov. 5, at the Pensacola Museum of History will feature costumed interpreters portraying key figures spanning from Don Tristán de Luna's 1559 arrival through the American…
item.content:encoded:
Pensacola's past will take center stage next week when Fiesta Pensacola presents its Living Museum experience as part of the Foo Foo Festival. The immersive event Thursday, Nov. 5, at the Pensacola Museum of History will feature costumed interpreters portraying key figures spanning from Don Tristán de Luna's 1559 arrival through the American Revolution and beyond.

Visitors will encounter historical personalities including Andrew and Rachel Jackson, Spanish settlers, local icons, and aviation pioneer Jacqueline Cochran. The experience also includes stops at a recreation of Trader Jon's bar and exhibits focused on the American Revolution era, with actors like Benedict Arnold and Spanish General Bernardo de Gálvez bringing those stories to life through first-person storytelling and interactive performances.

Bridget Middleton, executive director of Fiesta Pensacola, said the Living Museum fulfills the organization's mission to celebrate the city's heritage while building community pride. "We're excited to allow visitors to step into Pensacola's remarkable history and experience these stories in a way that is both educational and entertaining," she said.

The event runs from 5:30 to 8 p.m. Thursday at the museum, located at 330 S. Jefferson St. in downtown Pensacola. An outdoor pre-reception with appetizers, refreshments and live music begins at 5:30 p.m., with the museum experience starting at 6 p.m. Admission is $8 for adults, $5 for children ages 5-12, and free for younger children. Advance tickets are available online through the Foo Foo Festival website.

item.title: NAS Pensacola Edges Korean Navy in Friendly Soccer Match
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Naval Air Station Pensacola's tenant command team defeated sailors from the visiting Republic of Korea Ship Hansando 4-2 in a friendly soccer match Monday at the Barrancas Sports Complex, according to a Navy press release. The 11-on-11 game saw the NAS Pensacola side rally from an early two-goal deficit, with Naval Aviation Schools Command Ensign…
item.content:encoded:
Naval Air Station Pensacola's tenant command team defeated sailors from the visiting Republic of Korea Ship Hansando 4-2 in a friendly soccer match Monday at the Barrancas Sports Complex, according to a Navy press release. The 11-on-11 game saw the NAS Pensacola side rally from an early two-goal deficit, with Naval Aviation Schools Command Ensign Andrew Schuetz scoring twice to spark the comeback.

The match, organized by NAS Pensacola's Morale, Welfare and Recreation Department, was part of a broader cultural and professional exchange during the Hansando's four-day port visit through October 29. NAS Pensacola MWR Sports Coordinator Brett Pelfrey said the event highlighted how sports serve as a universal language, fostering camaraderie between the two allied nations. "Seeing these players interact not only on the pitch but in the celebrations after was a rewarding experience," Pelfrey said in a statement.

The Hansando and its embarked Cruise Task Training Group arrived at NAS Pensacola on October 26, marking a significant visit during the naval air station's 200th anniversary year. Beyond the soccer match, ROK Navy sailors and midshipmen participated in a wreath-laying ceremony at the Korean War Memorial in downtown Pensacola, toured the National Naval Aviation Museum, and observed a Blue Angels practice demonstration. Players from both teams exchanged jerseys following the match.

Blue Wahoos Stadium, home to Pensacola's minor league baseball team, regularly hosts college games and other events beyond the regular season schedule. The facility's hosting of marquee college programs like Ohio State and UConn underscores its role as a regional sports venue.

item.title: USDA Awards $325M to 42 Conservation Projects Nationwide, Including Florida Initiatives
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: The U.S. Department of Agriculture announced Wednesday a $325 million investment across 42 projects aimed at helping farmers, ranchers, and forest landowners improve operations while protecting natural resources, according to a news release from the USDA's Natural Resources Conservation Service. The funding flows through the Regional Conservation…
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture announced Wednesday a $325 million investment across 42 projects aimed at helping farmers, ranchers, and forest landowners improve operations while protecting natural resources, according to a news release from the USDA's Natural Resources Conservation Service.

The funding flows through the Regional Conservation Partnership Program (RCPP), which pairs federal dollars with private investment to address environmental challenges on agricultural land. USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins said the program reflects the administration's commitment to supporting American farming while reducing regulatory burden. "The Regional Conservation Partnership Program pairs private investment with federal funds to deliver better results," Rollins said in a statement.

Among the projects highlighted is Iowa's Cattle and Conservation Working Lands Program, which will expand across western and central Iowa. That effort aims to plant more than 300,000 acres of cover crops and reduce nitrogen runoff by roughly 3.3 million pounds while cutting phosphorus pollution by 336,000 pounds and soil loss by 1 million tons. Another project in southwest Georgia will protect at least 6,000 acres of working forest through voluntary conservation easements.

The Working Families Tax Cuts Act provides the largest long-term investment in NRCS conservation programs in decades, with support for RCPP through fiscal year 2031. The USDA said the program empowers local partners to address resource challenges unique to their regions while strengthening farm profitability and resilience.
